Background chicken meat extract is a popular functional food in Asia. It is rich in the bioactive compounds carnosine and anserine, two histidine-containing dipeptides (HCD). Studies suggest that acute pre-exercise ingestion of chicken extracts has important applications towards exercise performance and fatigue control, but the evidence is equivocal. This study aimed to evaluate the ergogenic potential of the pre-exercise ingestion of a homemade chicken broth (CB) vs a placebo soup on a short-lasting, high-intensity cycling exercise. Methods fourteen men participated in this double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover intervention study. Subjects ingested either CB, thereby receiving 46.4 mg/kg body weight of HCD, or a placebo soup (similar in taste without HCD) 40 min before an 8 min cycling time trial (TT) was performed. Venous blood samples were collected at arrival (fasted), before exercise and at 5 min recovery. Plasma HCD were measured with UPLC-MS/MS and glutathione (in red blood cells) was measured through HPLC. Capillary blood samples were collected at different timepoints before and after exercise. Results a significant improvement ( p = 0.033; 5.2%) of the 8 min TT mean power was observed after CB supplementation compared to placebo. Post-exercise plasma carnosine ( p < 0.05) and anserine ( p < 0.001) was significantly increased after CB supplementation and not following placebo. No significant effect of CB supplementation was observed either on blood glutathione levels, nor on capillary blood analysis. Conclusions oral CB supplementation improved the 8 min TT performance albeit it did not affect the acid-base balance or oxidative status parameters. Further research should unravel the potential role and mechanisms of HCD, present in CB, in this ergogenic approach. Keywords Carnosine Anserine Chicken broth Pre-exercise meal High-intensity exercise Performance Industrial Research Fund (IOF, Ghent University) F2014/IOF-StarTT/273 Derave Wim issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2021 Background Chicken meat and its extracts have long been recognized as a source of bioactive molecules that can potentially improve health status in general, and exercise performance in particular. In traditional South-Asian medicine, chicken extracts are used to alleviate stress or mild disease symptoms [ 1 ]. The activities of chicken extracts are suggested to be related to its active components, including proteins, free amino acids, taurine, many minerals, trace elements, and vitamins. In addition, chicken meat extracts contain high concentrations of carnosine (β-alanyl-L-histidine) and anserine (β-alanyl-π-methyl-histidine) in a 1:2 to 1:3 ratio [ 2 , 3 ]. Carnosine and its methylated analogue anserine are histidine-containing dipeptides (HCD) present in high concentrations in skeletal muscle of mammals and therefore abundantly present in the daily food of non-vegetarian persons [ 2 ]. Harris et al. [ 4 ] demonstrated that long-term administration of β-alanine - one of the constituent amino acids - is able to raise muscle carnosine concentrations, which leads to enhanced high-intensity exercise performance [ 5 , 6 ]. The chronic use of chicken breast extract, containing carnosine and anserine, is shown to enhance muscle carnosine levels in humans [ 7 ] and to improve high-intensity endurance performance by attenuation of muscle fatigue [ 8 ], demonstrating the same mechanism of action of the β-alanine supplementation approach. In contrast to chronic supplementation strategies, aiming to promote muscle carnosine loading (thus increasing the intracellular muscle pH-buffer capacity), it can be hypothesized that acute supplementation, leading to elevated circulating HCD, may exert ergogenic effects through attenuation of acidosis and/or oxidative stress in blood. Unfortunately, the bioavailability of carnosine in the circulation following supplementation is very low in humans due to the fast breakdown by the very active human serum carnosinase-1 (CN1) enzyme, and acute carnosine supplementation (20 mg/kg BW) could not elicit improvements in a high-intensity cycling test [ 9 ]. Interestingly, both in vitro [ 3 , 10 , 11 ] and in vivo [ 12 , 13 ] experiments revealed that anserine is much less prone to hydrolysis by carnosinase due to the lower affinity to the CN1 enzyme, suggesting that anserine or a combination of anserine plus carnosine might be required to induce acute ergogenic effects. A recent study of Blancquaert et al. (unpublished, congress presentation: http://hdl.handle.net/1854/LU-8642579 ) demonstrated increased HCD stability in the circulation by a combination of pure (chemically synthesized) carnosine and anserine ingestion in a 1:1 ratio (25 mg/kg BW of each) compared to anserine alone (25 mg/kg BW). In addition, performance-enhancing effects of this pre-exercise supplementation strategy were found on maximal Wingate power in healthy humans. The ergogenic potential of acute pre-exercise supplementation of chicken extracts (containing both carnosine and anserine) is already tested by Suzuki and colleagues, but the results are so far inconclusive. Suzuki et al. [ 14 ] showed that the pre-exercise intake of the chicken breast extract (denominated as CBEX™), containing 0.4 g carnosine and 1.1 g anserine, enhanced the power output of the latter half of 2 sets of repeated sprints. In a follow-up study using the same supplementation strategy for a single set of similar repeated sprints, no improvement on performance was found, although a positive effect on exercise-induced acid-base balance was present [ 15 ]. Informed by this emerging evidence for an acute effect of pre-exercise supplementation of pure HCD on exercise performance, we evaluated the effect of a similar dose of HCD in a functional food approach, i.e. through a home-prepared chicken broth (CB) vs a placebo soup (PLA), in a cross-over nutritional intervention study. The purpose of this study is to examine the ergogenic effect of the chicken broth (CB), according to the recipe from Harris et al. [ 4 ], administered as a 40-min pre-exercise snack, on a short-lasting, high-intensity cycling exercise (8 min cycling time-trial). The type and duration of the exercise were aimed to challenge the possible ergogenic effects of anserine and carnosine in the CB based on their contribution to the intracellular acid-base balance as well as oxidative stress control [ 16 , 17 ].

extracted_data.document_summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study investigated the ergogenic effects of acute pre-exercise homemade chicken broth (CB) ingestion, rich in histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs) like carnosine and anserine, on high-intensity cycling performance in recreationally-trained men. The study found a significant 5.2% improvement in 8-minute time trial mean power and elevated plasma carnosine and anserine levels following CB supplementation. However, the ergogenic effect was not mediated by changes in acid-base balance or red blood cell glutathione status, indicating alternative mechanisms may be at play.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute pre-exercise nutritional supplementation (homemade chicken broth or placebo soup)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects ingested either 8 mL/kg body weight of homemade chicken broth (CB), providing 46.4 mg/kg body weight of total histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs) (specifically 15.6 mg/kg BW carnosine and 30.8 mg/kg BW anserine), or an equivalent volume of a placebo soup. The supplement was administered 25-40 minutes prior to an 8-minute high-intensity cycling time trial, following a warm-up. No dose-response comparisons were made, only CB versus placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant improvement (p = 0.033; 5.2%) after chicken broth supplementation compared to placebo. It resulted in a 5.2% higher mean power output.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents the integrated physiological output and capacity for high-intensity exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: High-intensity cycling time-trial performance following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Directly indicates improved high-intensity exercise performance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased post-exercise (p < 0.05, and p = 0.011 for interaction effect) after chicken broth supplementation compared to placebo, reaching 372.7 nmol/L at 5 min recovery post-exercise from a basal pooled plasma concentration of 23.34     ± 2.78 nmol/L. The increase in plasma carnosine was 50 times lower compared to plasma anserine, contributing to an almost 700-fold increase in total plasma HCDs (from 30 nmol/L to 20 µmol/L).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A histidine-containing dipeptide (HCD) involved in intracellular pH buffering, antioxidant activity, and oxidative stress control. It is degraded by serum carnosinase-1 (CN1).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise (53 min after supplementation) following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion and an 8-minute high-intensity cycling time trial.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated circulating levels are associated with potential ergogenic effects and improved high-intensity exercise performance through attenuation of acidosis and/or oxidative stress in blood. Its accumulation in plasma is interrelated with anserine accumulation and overall improved exercise performance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased post-exercise (p < 0.001 for both direct effect and interaction effect) after chicken broth supplementation compared to placebo, reaching 20,424.7 nmol/L at 5 min recovery post-exercise from a basal pooled plasma concentration of 7.93     ± 4.40 nmol/L. This increase was 50 times higher than that of plasma carnosine, contributing to an almost 700-fold increase in total plasma HCDs. Higher CN1 activity was negatively correlated with anserine accumulation (r = -0.692; p = 0.011).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A histidine-containing dipeptide (HCD), the methylated analogue of carnosine, involved in intracellular pH buffering, antioxidant activity, and oxidative stress control. It is degraded less efficiently by serum carnosinase-1 (CN1) than carnosine.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise (53 min after supplementation) following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion and an 8-minute high-intensity cycling time trial.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated circulating levels are associated with potential ergogenic effects and improved high-intensity exercise performance through attenuation of acidosis and/or oxidative stress in blood, particularly due to its increased stability in circulation. Its high elevation following CB supplementation suggests it is a key metabolic marker responsive to the supplement.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant effect of chicken broth supplementation was observed on red blood cell reduced glutathione (GSH, p = 0.771) or oxidized glutathione disulphide (GSSG, p = 0.267) levels. No main effect of time or supplement was present.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A major antioxidant system protecting cells from oxidative damage and maintaining cellular redox balance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After pre-exercise chicken broth supplementation and a high-intensity cycling time-trial, sampled at fasted, pre-warm-up, and post-exercise time points.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Unaffected by CB supplementation, suggesting it does not significantly alter the glutathione status in red blood cells under the study conditions, and thus is not a primary mediator of the observed performance effects through antioxidant capacities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant effects of chicken broth supplementation were observed on blood pH. During the time-trial, pH naturally declined from 7.4 to 7.2.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of acid-base balance in the blood, essential for physiological processes and enzyme function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During an 8-min high-intensity cycling time-trial following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Unchanged pH indicates that the ergogenic effect of chicken broth is not mediated through improved extracellular pH buffering during high-intensity exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant effects of chicken broth supplementation were observed on blood lactate levels. During the time-trial, lactate levels naturally increased from 1 to 16 mmol/L.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A byproduct of anaerobic metabolism, serving as an energy substrate and associated with muscle fatigue.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During an 8-min high-intensity cycling time-trial following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Unchanged lactate levels suggest that the ergogenic effect of chicken broth is not due to altered lactate production or clearance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant effects of chicken broth supplementation were observed on blood bicarbonate levels. During the time-trial, bicarbonate levels naturally declined from 25 to 12 mmol/L. Plasma concentrations of bicarbonate are approximately 25 mmol/L, which is 1000-fold higher than the observed increase in plasma HCDs.
